To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1)some plant species in mountainous regions may shift downslope back towards low elevations where they had been previously harvested, and (2) this downslope shift can damp or even reverse climate-driven upslope shifts, and (3) the cessation-driven downslope shift is more important than the climate-driven upslope shift in our study area.

(1), in mountainous regions, the cessation of historical disturbances can cause downslope shifts of plant species distributions; (2), these downslope shifts may dampen or even reverse climate-driven upslope shifts of plant distributions; and (3), in the context of global change, the effects of land-use change on plant distributions should be explicitly considered in addition to the effects of rising temperatures.

(1)cessation-driven forest recovery may dampen or reverse the effects of climate change on species shifts, and (2) in mountainous areas that are recovering from historical disturbances, the cessation of disturbances and consequent recovery may have greater effects on species shifts than warming climate.
